doc_description: Lockheed Martin Corporation’s Form 10‑K for the year ended December 31, 2021 (NYSE: LMT) reports $67.0B in sales (71% from the U.S. Government), four-segment operations anchored by the F‑35 (27% of total), a $135.4B backlog, a $1.7B noncash pension settlement charge, and key risks including the FTC‑contested Aerojet Rocketdyne acquisition, with audited financials and effective internal controls attested.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- SEC filing: Lockheed Martin Corporation Form 10‑K for fiscal year ended December 31, 2021; includes corporate details (state of incorporation: Maryland; EIN; headquarters address; phone), stock listing (NYSE: LMT), share count, market value, filer status (well-known seasoned issuer, large accelerated filer), internal control attestation, and incorporation by reference of the 2022 Definitive Proxy Statement into Part III.
- Table of Contents outlining Parts I–IV with standard 10-K items: Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Executive Officers; Market for Equity and Buybacks; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Controls and Procedures; Other Information; Foreign jurisdiction inspection disclosures; Governance; Executive Compensation; Ownership; Related-party matters; Audit fees; Exhibits; and 10‑K Summary.
- Business overview (Part I, Item 1): Describes Lockheed Martin as a global security and aerospace company focused on research, design, development, manufacture, integration, and sustainment of advanced technology systems and services across defense, civil, and commercial markets.
- Customer and sales mix for 2021: $67.0B net sales with 71% from the U.S. Government (including 62% from DoD), 28% from international customers (including FMS), and 1% from U.S. commercial/other.
- Strategic context: Operating amid complex global security and economic pressures; emphasis on program execution, affordability, predictable delivery, disciplined expansion into adjacent markets, growth in international sales, investment in talent and innovative technologies, and use of acquisitions, partnerships, joint ventures, and equity investments.
- Business segments: Four segments—Aeronautics; Missiles and Fire Control (MFC); Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS); and Space.
- Pending acquisition: Agreement to acquire Aerojet Rocketdyne Holdings, Inc. for $51/share (post-dividend equity value approx. $4.6B); regulatory review status with FTC second request; FTC likely to sue to block; options to defend or terminate; potential closing timing and outside date (March 21, 2022); related risks referenced in Risk Factors.
- Aeronautics segment details: 2021 net sales of $26.7B (40% of total); customers primarily U.S. Air Force and U.S. Navy plus international; sales mix 65% U.S. Government and 35% international; combat aircraft products/services represented ~32% of total consolidated net sales in 2019 and 2021 (33% in 2020).

structure.summary:
- Company overview: A global security and aerospace firm focused on research, design, development, manufacture, integration, and sustainment of advanced technology systems, plus a wide range of engineering, logistics, systems integration, and cybersecurity services for U.S. and international defense, civil, and commercial markets.
- 2021 sales mix: $67.0B total; 71% U.S. Government (including 62% DoD), 28% international (including FMS via the U.S. Government), 1% U.S. commercial/other.
- Strategic priorities: Emphasis on disciplined program execution, affordability, rapid delivery of capability, targeted growth in adjacent markets and internationally, investment in workforce skills and internal innovation, and continued M&A and partnerships/joint ventures/equity investments with commercial industry.
- Operating environment: Complex global security landscape and ongoing U.S./global economic pressures shaping execution and affordability initiatives.
- Business structure: Four segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space—organized by product/service lines.
- Pending acquisition: Agreement to acquire Aerojet Rocketdyne for $51.00 per share (post-dividend), implying ~$4.6B equity value and ~$4.4B transaction value; shareholder approval received March 9, 2021; FTC “second request” completed; FTC signaled concerns not resolvable via proposed consent terms and likely to sue to block before Jan 27, 2022; parties could defend the suit or terminate; outside date to close or terminate is March 21, 2022; related risks referenced in Item 1A.
- Aeronautics segment snapshot (2021): $26.7B in net sales (40% of consolidated); customers include U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy, other U.S. agencies, and international/commercial buyers; sales mix 65% U.S. Government, 35% international; combat aircraft accounted for 32% of total consolidated net sales in 2019 and 2021 (33% in 2020).

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: ITEM 1. Business
structure.start_phrase:
We are a global security and aerospace company principally engaged in the research, design, development, manufacture, integration and sustainment of advanced
technology systems, products and services.
structure.summary:
- Company overview: Global security and aerospace company serving primarily the U.S. Government with defense, civil, and commercial applications. 2021 net sales mix: 71% U.S. Government (62% DoD), 28% international, 1% U.S. commercial. Strategic focus on program execution, affordability, disciplined growth in adjacent and international markets, internal innovation, acquisitions/partnerships.
- Business structure: Four segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space—organized by products/services.
- Pending acquisition: Agreement to acquire Aerojet Rocketdyne; extensive FTC review including a second request; FTC signaled intent to block; potential litigation or termination by March 21, 2022.
- Aeronautics (40% of 2021 net sales): Advanced military aircraft R&D, production, sustainment, and classified programs.
  - F-35 (largest program): 27% of total company sales, 68% of Aeronautics; multiple development/production/sustainment contracts; 142 aircraft delivered in 2021 (753 to date), continued COVID-19 impacts; delivery outlook 148–153 in 2022, 156 thereafter; 230-aircraft backlog.
  - C-130J: 22 delivered in 2021; 79-aircraft backlog into 2025.
  - F-16: International production and upgrades; 128-aircraft backlog into 2027.
  - F-22: Ongoing modernization and sustainment for USAF.
  - Advanced Development Programs (Skunk Works): Unmanned/manned systems, hypersonics, ISR, situational awareness, air mobility, and network-enabled capabilities.
- Missiles and Fire Control (17%): Air/missile defense, tactical missiles, fire control, logistics, mission ops, classified programs.
  - Key programs: PAC-3, THAAD; MLRS, Hellfire, JASSM; Apache fire control, SNIPER, IRST21; SOF GLSS; hypersonics with USAF/Army.
- Rotary and Mission Systems (25%): Military/commercial helicopters; naval combat and missile defense systems; radar; C6ISR; cyber; training and logistics; classified work.
  - Key programs: Sikorsky (Black Hawk/Seahawk, CH-53K, CRH, VH-92A); IWSS (Aegis, LCS, MMSC); C6ISR (C2BMC, undersea combat systems); TLS (sustainment, simulators/training).
- Space (18%): Satellites, space transportation, strategic and defensive systems, ground systems integration, classified systems.
  - Key programs: SBIRS and Next Gen OPIR; Trident II D5 FBM; Orion; GPS III; hypersonics (Army/Navy); Next Generation Interceptor.
  - Note: UK renationalized AWE program in 2021, removing it from results.
- Intellectual property: Extensive IP portfolio; U.S. Government rights under FAR/DFARS; no single IP right is critical to the business.
- Research and development: Company-funded IR&D and customer-funded R&D across basic/applied research, design, development, and testing.
- Supply chain and materials: Reliance on aluminum, titanium, carbon fiber, advanced microelectronics (including semiconductors). Long-term agreements help supply continuity; COVID-19 and market volatility pose risks. Business not seasonal; timing of awards, funding, deliveries affects period sales.
- Human capital: ~114,000 employees (93% U.S.; ~59,000 engineers/scientists/IT; ~20% union). Focus on talent acquisition/retention, early-career pipelines, engagement, competitive pay/benefits, flexible telework, development and succession.
  - Diversity and inclusion: Business Resource Groups; improved representation. U.S. profile (self-identified): Women 23% (executives 23%), People of Color 29% (15%), Veterans 21% (20%), People with Disabilities 10% (11%).
  - Safety and health: Metrics-driven program; COVID-19 protocols, flexible telework, vaccination encouragement.
- Competition: Against large primes, smaller firms, startups, non-traditional defense entrants; competition factors include value, technical/management capability, integration, total cost, execution, speed, and emerging tech (additive mfg, AI, digital engineering, autonomy, commercial space). International sales influenced by export controls and offset requirements.
- Government contracts and regulations: Extensive compliance (FAR/DFARS, cost/pricing data, cost accounting, export controls, cybersecurity, approved business systems). Government termination rights (convenience/default). Use of undefinitized contract actions with potential unilateral definitization. Significant classified work with comparable risks to unclassified programs.
- Environmental and climate: Ongoing remediation at certain sites; costs largely allowable under U.S. Government contracts. Growing climate/GHG regulatory focus; potential for increased compliance costs; corporate sustainability targets.
- Corporate and investor information: Company background and headquarters; access to SEC filings via company and SEC websites; availability of reports.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautionary statements regarding projections and risks; safe harbor language.
- Initial risk factors highlighted:
  - Heavy reliance on U.S. Government funding; exposure to appropriations cycles, continuing resolutions, shutdowns, debt ceiling, and changing priorities domestically and abroad.
  - F-35 concentration risk and program-specific challenges (supplier performance including COVID-19 impacts, software, testing, sustainment costs, unit cost reductions, and funding timing).
  - Dependence on government authorization/funding for growth areas (hypersonics, classified, next-gen programs).

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: ITEM 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase: An investment in our common stock or debt securities involves risks and uncertainties.
structure.summary:
- The document contains forward-looking statements subject to safe harbor protections.
- Item 1A: Risk Factors emphasizes:
  - Heavy reliance on U.S. Government contracts (71% of 2021 sales; 62% DoD) and exposure to budget uncertainty, debt ceiling, continuing resolutions, and shutdowns.
  - Concentration risk in the F-35 program (27% of 2021 sales) with challenges in supplier performance, software, modernization, sustainment affordability, schedule, cost, testing, and COVID-19 impacts.
  - Compliance with complex procurement laws and regulations, including government rights to terminate for convenience/default, use of Undefinitized Contract Actions, and option-year risks.
  - Evolving procurement policies increasing cost emphasis, preference for fixed-price (including on development) and rapid acquisition/OTAs, potential changes to progress payment rates, and related margin/cash flow risks.
  - Profitability variability driven by contract mix (fixed-price vs. cost-reimbursable), inflation, LRIP transition risks, and performance-based incentives; potential penalties and forfeitures in certain Space contracts.
  - Routine audits/investigations (DCAA/DCMA/IG) leading to payment withholds, cost allowability disputes, possible penalties, and reputational harm.
  - Heightened competition, multi-award IDIQ dynamics, pricing pressure, bid protests, industry consolidation/vertical integration, and competition from startups/non-traditional defense firms.
  - Ongoing COVID-19 impacts on costs, supply chain, workforce (including vaccine mandates and attrition risk), travel/site access, and schedule; monitoring for potential asset impairments.
  - Dependence on subcontractors/suppliers/teammates; risks from rare earths (China), semiconductor shortages, single/limited sources, qualification lead times, and supply chain cybersecurity/compliance burdens.
  - Need for continuous innovation and efficient production; risks in development programs, partnerships with commercial tech firms (IP/liability differences), and securing next-gen/hypersonics/classified opportunities.
  - International sales risks (28% of 2021 sales): FMS vs. DCS regimes, export controls, FCPA/anti-corruption, anti-boycott, taxation, currency, local procurement laws, and offset/industrial participation obligations with potential penalties.
  - Geopolitical exposures, including potential Chinese sanctions related to Taiwan sales, trade restrictions, and U.S. foreign policy actions affecting approvals and timing.
  - U.S. sanctions on Turkey: removal from F-35 program, supplier transitions, licensing denials impacting the Turkish Utility Helicopter Program (TUHP), possible restructurings/terminations/penalties; currently not material overall but poses localized risks and costs.
  - Intellectual property risks: government rights under FAR/DFARS, evolving DoD IP policies, supplier IP licensing challenges, and third-party infringement claims.
  - Talent acquisition/retention challenges for cleared, technical, cyber, and leadership roles; competition with commercial tech firms; hybrid work risks; union negotiations/work stoppage exposure.
  - Cybersecurity and physical security threats (including nation-state actors), supply chain cyber risks, potential data/IP compromise, operational disruptions, customer confidence impacts, and uninsured costs.
  - M&A/joint venture/venture investment risks, including due diligence, integration, successor liability, impairments, and shared-control challenges; detailed uncertainty around the proposed Aerojet Rocketdyne acquisition and potential FTC litigation, integration, financing, and synergy risks.
  - Pension and postretirement plan volatility driven by discount rates, asset returns, mortality, funding timing; pension risk transfer transactions and potential settlement charges/insurer default risk.
  - Estimation and impairment risks, particularly goodwill (notably Sikorsky) and long-term contract accounting judgments.
  - Tax risks from law changes and audits; 2022 R&D capitalization rule could reduce cash from operations by an estimated ~$500 million absent retroactive relief; potential effects of corporate tax rate increases.
  - Limits of insurance/indemnities for product liability, unusually hazardous risks, and natural disasters; climate change may exacerbate hazards and costs; concentration in higher-risk geographies.
  - Environmental compliance and remediation liabilities, evolving standards, cost allowability issues, and climate-related regulation/procurement changes that may increase costs or affect competitiveness; potential for climate-related litigation.
  - Legal proceedings outcomes are uncertain and may affect results.
  - Discretionary nature of dividends and share repurchases; potential constraints from earnings, cash flows, and stockholders’ equity.
- Item 1B: Unresolved Staff Comments: None.
- Item 2: Properties overview:
  - Approximately 362 owned/leased sites (offices, plants, warehouses, labs) plus management/occupancy of ~10 government-owned facilities.
  - Major locations by segment include:
    - Aeronautics: Palmdale, CA; Marietta, GA; Greenville, SC; Fort Worth, TX.
    - Missiles and Fire Control: Camden, AR; Ocala/Orlando, FL; Lexington, KY; Grand Prairie, TX.
    - Rotary and Mission Systems: Shelton/Stratford, CT; Orlando, FL; Moorestown/Mt. Laurel, NJ; Owego/Syracuse, NY; Manassas, VA; Mielec, Poland.
    - Space: Huntsville, AL; Sunnyvale, CA; Denver, CO; Cape Canaveral, FL; Valley Forge, PA.
    - Corporate: Bethesda, MD.

structure.start_phrase:
The following Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations (MD&A) is intended to help the reader understand our results
of operations and financial condition.
structure.summary:
- Scope and context: MD&A covers 2021 performance with 2020 comparisons; 2019 discussion referenced to prior 10-K.
- Company overview: Global security and aerospace firm with four segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space. 2021 net sales $67.0B; customer mix: 71% U.S. Government (62% DoD), 28% international (incl. FMS), 1% U.S. commercial. Strategy emphasizes program execution, affordability, disciplined portfolio expansion, internal R&D, M&A, and industry partnerships.
- COVID-19: Ongoing impacts across business areas (supplier delays, travel/site restrictions, workforce effects). Continued supplier support via accelerated payments ($2.2B outstanding accelerations at 12/31/21). Vaccine mandate landscape monitored; potential workforce/supplier attrition risk if mandates reinstated. Future pandemic effects remain uncertain.
- 2022 outlook: Net sales expected to decrease ~2%, driven by AWE renationalization (Space), non-repeat of an RMS training system, and lower SOF GLSS volume (MFC). Segment operating margin ~10.9%; cash from operations ≥ $7.9B assuming no pension contributions and potential ~$500M cash impact from required R&D capitalization. Assumes 21% U.S. tax rate, continued program funding, no extended CR, continued supplier payment acceleration. Expected 2022 net FAS/CAS pension benefit ~$2.3B; no required pension contributions.
- Portfolio shaping:
  - AWE renationalization (UK) effective 6/30/21; 2021 AWE sales $885M and OP $18M included in Space through that date (2020: $1.4B sales, $35M OP).
  - Pending Aerojet Rocketdyne acquisition (~$4.4B transaction value post-dividend): FTC review ongoing; high likelihood of litigation to block; potential close/termination options before 3/21/22 termination date.
- U.S. Government funding: FY22 NDAA enacted with ~$25B above request; appropriations pending with CRs through 2/18/22; debt ceiling raised to $31.4T. CRs can delay procurement/new starts.
- International business: Growth focus via FMS and DCS. Key interests:
  - Aeronautics: F-35, F-16, C-130J.
  - MFC: PAC‑3, THAAD, tactical/strike missiles (LRASM, JASSM).
  - RMS: Aegis and surface combatants, MMSC, training/logistics, Black Hawk/Seahawk/CH‑53K international sales (e.g., Israel LOA for 12 CH‑53K).
  - Space: AWE through 6/30/21.
- F-35 program: U.S. services objective 2,456 aircraft; partners and FMS customers engaged. Cumulative 753 deliveries through 2021; 142 delivered in 2021 (exceeding plan); plan 148–153 in 2022 and 156 annually from 2023; backlog 230 aircraft. Ongoing challenges include supply chain/COVID, software, funding timing, testing, sustainment cost, and affordability.
- Backlog: $135.4B at 12/31/21 (vs. $147.1B prior year); funded backlog $88.5B (vs. $102.3B). Expect ~38% revenue conversion within 12 months, ~60% within 24 months.
- Consolidated results (2021 vs. 2020): Net sales $67.0B (+3); operating profit $9.1B; EPS $22.76; effective tax rate 16.4%. Product sales 84%, services 16%. Notable items: $1.7B noncash pension settlement charge (driving non‑service FAS pension expense), Ventures fair value gains, lower interest expense, prior-year AMMROC impairment. 2020 discontinued ops tax-related loss $55M.
- Segment performance and 2022 trends:
  - Aeronautics: Sales $26.7B, OP $2.8B. Drivers: higher classified and F‑16; lower F‑35 development; F‑22 sustainment down. $225M loss on a classified program. 2022: low-single digit growth in sales and OP; margin in line.
  - MFC: Sales $11.7B, OP $1.65B. Drivers: higher PAC‑3, LRASM, JASSM; partial reversal of Warrior losses; a ~$25M energy program charge. 2022: low-single digit decline in sales and OP; slight margin improvement.
  - RMS: Sales $16.8B, OP $1.80B. Drivers: higher Sikorsky production (Black Hawk, CH‑53K, CRH), international pilot training system; mixed IWSS volume. 2022: low-single digit sales decline; high-single digit OP decline; lower margin.
  - Space: Sales $11.8B, OP $1.13B. Drivers: AWE renationalization down; higher hypersonics/NGI and Next Gen OPIR/SBIRS; lower ULA equity earnings; ~$80M charge on a commercial ground solutions program. 2022: mid-single digit sales decline; high-single digit OP decline; lower margin.
- Pension FAS/CAS: Net FAS/CAS adjustment $668M in 2021 (impacted by the $1.7B settlement charge). Expect 2022 FAS pension income ~$460M and net FAS/CAS pension benefit ~$2.3B; no 2022 contributions.
- Liquidity and cash flows: Cash $3.6B; strong access to credit. 2021 CFO $9.2B (up on lower pension contributions and higher noncash-adjusted earnings), investing cash use $1.2B (lower capex; AMMROC JV sale proceeds), financing cash use $7.6B (higher buybacks/dividends; $500M debt maturity repaid). 2021 buybacks $4.1B; dividends $10.60/share; new $5B repurchase authorization (remaining $3.9B at year-end). Ongoing supplier payment accelerations; progress payments at 90% continue to support cash.
- Capital structure and resources: Net debt ~$11.7B (fixed-rate notes); covenant compliant; revolving credit and commercial paper access.
- Contractual commitments and contingencies: Total obligations ~$83.4B (debt/interest, leases, purchase obligations incl. ~$52.8B tied to U.S. Government contracts), offset obligations ~$17.0B notional (potential penalties ~$1.7B), standby letters of credit/surety/guarantees ~$3.6B.
- Critical accounting policies:
  - Revenue recognition on long-term contracts (ASC 606): predominant over-time, cost‑to‑cost; treatment of fixed‑price vs. cost‑reimbursable; performance obligations, variable consideration, and contract modifications; reliance on estimates and profit booking rate adjustments; FAR cost allowability; DCAA oversight.
- Postretirement benefit plans: Significant plans with volatility mitigation via pension risk transfers; 2021 annuity purchase transferring $4.9B obligations (noncash $1.7B settlement). Key assumptions: 2.875% discount rate; 6.5% expected return; updated longevity increased obligations modestly. Sensitivities provided. ERISA funded status ~92% at YE21; CAS recoveries $2.1B (2021), prepayment credits ~$7.0B; ARPA lowers funding/CAS costs.
- Environmental matters: Liabilities $742M with $645M recoverable from U.S. Government pricing; long-duration remediation estimates; potential material increases from tighter standards for hexavalent chromium, perchlorate, and PFAS; PRP cost sharing and potential recoveries.
- Goodwill and intangibles: Annual impairment testing—no impairments in 2021; Sikorsky reporting unit fair value ~30% above carrying value but remains at risk if cash flows deteriorate. Finite-lived intangibles amortized; no indefinite-lived impairments.
- Market risk and hedging: Exposure to interest rates, FX (GBP, EUR, CAD, AUD, NOK, PLN), and equity markets; use of derivatives (interest rate swaps, FX forwards/options); notional balances disclosed; impacts not material; deferred compensation trust market exposure partially offset by liabilities.

nodes.title: Revenue Recognition
nodes.heading: Revenue Recognition –
nodes.start_phrase: The majority of our net sales are generated from long-term contracts with the U.S. Government and international customers (including foreign military sales (FMS) contracted through the U.S. Government) for the research, design, development, manufacture, integration and sustainment of advanced technology systems, products and services.
nodes.summary:
- Overview of Lockheed Martin’s business: a global security and aerospace company serving U.S. and international customers, operating in four segments—Aeronautics, Missiles and Fire Control (MFC), Rotary and Mission Systems (RMS), and Space.
- AWE program renationalization: UK Ministry of Defence assumed control on June 30, 2021; AWE results included in Space through date of transfer—2021 sales $885 million and operating profit $18 million; 2020 sales $1.4 billion and operating profit $35 million.
- Basis of presentation: consolidation of controlled subsidiaries and variable interest entities where the company is primary beneficiary; elimination of intercompany transactions; classification of certain assets/liabilities as current based on contract operating cycle (often >1 year).
- Use of estimates: extensive judgments under U.S. GAAP affecting sales/cost recognition, postretirement benefits, environmental matters, asset impairments (goodwill, intangibles, investments), income taxes, fair value, and contingencies.
- Revenue recognition policies:
  - Contract types: fixed-price (including performance-based incentives) and cost-reimbursable (cost-plus-award-fee, cost-plus-incentive-fee, cost-plus-fixed-fee).
  - Contract combination and performance obligations: most contracts treated as a single performance obligation due to integration/complexity; limited cases with multiple obligations.
  - Transaction price: includes variable consideration at most likely amount, constrained to avoid significant reversal; modifications typically treated as part of existing contract.
  - Allocation to performance obligations: based on standalone selling prices; U.S. Government/FMS often equal to stated contract price under FAR; non-U.S. Government uses expected cost plus margin or observable prices.
  - Timing of revenue: predominantly over time via percentage-of-completion cost-to-cost due to continuous transfer of control (e.g., termination-for-convenience clauses for U.S. Government; no alternative use and right to payment for commercial contracts). Point-in-time recognition used when control does not transfer over time.
  - Backlog: defined as remaining performance obligations; $135.4 billion at December 31, 2021; ~38% expected to convert to revenue within 12 months and ~60% within 24 months.
  - Billing/payments: PBPs or progress payments for U.S. Government; advances and milestones for international direct contracts; contract liabilities for payments in excess of revenue; receivables and contract assets presentation.
  - Estimation and profit booking rates: ongoing assessment of sales, costs, technical/schedule risks, offsets/localization, and variable consideration; risk retirements or deteriorations drive margin adjustments; loss provisions recorded when total costs exceed transaction price.
  - Impact of estimate changes: non-volume net adjustments increased segment operating profit by ~$2.0B (2021), $1.8B (2020), $1.9B (2019); increased net earnings by ~$1.6B ($5.81/share) in 2021 and ~$1.5B ($5.33 and $5.29/share) in 2020 and 2019; revenue from prior-period performance obligations recognized of ~$2.2B (2021), $2.0B (2020), $2.2B (2019).
- Program-specific matters:
  - Aeronautics classified fixed-price incentive contract: $225 million loss recognized in Q2 2021; contract amended in Q4 2021 consistent with assumptions; potential for additional future losses; monitoring recoverability of precontract costs.
  - RMS ground-based radar: cumulative losses of ~$280 million as of December 31, 2021; further losses not expected to be material based on current estimates.
  - RMS EADGE-T international C4I program: cumulative losses of ~$260 million as of December 31, 2021; no additional material charges anticipated at this time.
- Research and development: includes company-funded (IR&D) and customer-funded; expensed as incurred; company-funded R&D charged to cost of sales—$1.5B (2021), $1.3B (2020 and 2019).
- Stock-based compensation: RSUs and PSUs (generally three-year vesting); fair value measured at grant (RSUs at market price less dividend timing discount; PSUs may use Monte Carlo); expense recognized ratably considering retirement eligibility and estimated forfeitures; performance-based PSU vesting estimates updated each period.
- Income taxes: asset-liability method for deferred taxes; evaluation of uncertain tax positions with recognition of largest more-likely-than-not benefit; interest/penalties recorded in tax expense; state/local taxes generally recorded in operating costs per government contract regulations.
- Cash and cash equivalents: instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
- Receivables: unconditional rights to consideration, recorded net of expected collections; no significant impairments in 2019–2021.
- Contract assets: unbilled receivables from over-time recognition where revenue exceeds billings; recorded at expected collectible amounts and classified as current based on contract operating cycle.

nodes.title: Research and development and similar costs
nodes.heading: Research and development and similar costs –
nodes.start_phrase: We conduct research and development (R&D) activities using our own funds (referred to as company-funded R&D or independent research and development (IR&D)) and under contractual arrangements with our customers (referred to as customer-funded R&D) to enhance existing products and services and to develop future technologies.
nodes.summary:
- Research and development costs: Distinguishes company-funded (IR&D) and customer-funded R&D; defines included activities; company-funded R&D allocated to G&A and generally recoverable on U.S. Government contracts; customer-funded charged directly to contracts; substantially all R&D expensed to cost of sales as incurred; disclosed amounts: $1.5 billion (2021) and $1.3 billion (2020, 2019).
- Stock-based compensation: Awards in RSUs and PSUs that generally vest in three years; fair value at grant date—RSUs at market price less dividend-equivalent discount; PSUs valued like RSUs or via Monte Carlo for market conditions; expense recognition net of estimated forfeitures—RSUs over requisite service period (considering retirement eligibility); PSUs with service/performance conditions recognized over vesting based on expected vesting; PSUs with market conditions recognized over vesting; forfeiture estimates and expected PSU vesting updated each reporting date.
- Income taxes: Asset-liability method; deferred tax assets/liabilities for temporary differences and carryforwards measured with enacted rates; uncertain tax positions recognized using more-likely-than-not threshold and largest benefit expected upon settlement; interest and penalties recorded in income tax expense; for government contracts, current state/local income and franchise taxes treated as allowable operating costs; changes in deferred state taxes and unrecognized state tax benefits recorded in unallocated corporate expenses.
- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
- Receivables: Unconditional rights to consideration (billed and currently due), recorded at net amount expected to be collected; no significant impairments in 2021, 2020, or 2019.
- Contract assets: Unbilled amounts from percentage-of-completion cost-to-cost method when revenue recognized exceeds billings; recorded at net amount expected to be billed and collected; classified as current based on contract operating cycle, even if billing/collection extends beyond one year due to long-cycle contracts.

nodes.title: Stock-based compensation

nodes.summary:
- Research and development: Distinguishes company-funded (IR&D) vs customer-funded R&D; company-funded R&D included in G&A and generally recoverable on U.S. Government contracts; customer-funded R&D charged directly to contracts; substantially all R&D expensed to cost of sales as incurred; disclosed amounts: $1.5B (2021), $1.3B (2020, 2019).

- Cash and cash equivalents: Highly liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
- Receivables: Unconditional rights to consideration (billed and due), recorded net of expected collections; no significant impairments in 2019–2021.

nodes.title: Income taxes
nodes.heading: Income taxes –
nodes.start_phrase: We calculate our provision for income taxes using the asset and liability method, under which deferred tax assets and liabilities are recognized based on the future tax consequences attributable to temporary differences that exist between the financial statement carrying amount of assets and liabilities and their respective tax bases, as well as from operating loss and tax credit carry-forwards.
nodes.summary:
- Outlines accounting policies for R&D, distinguishing company-funded (IR&D) versus customer-funded efforts; describes included activities, allocation of company-funded costs to G&A and recoverability on U.S. Government contracts; states all R&D is expensed to cost of sales as incurred; provides amounts for company-funded R&D ($1.5B in 2021; $1.3B in 2020 and 2019).
- Describes stock-based compensation for RSUs and PSUs that generally vest over three years; measurement at grant-date fair value (RSUs at market price less dividend-equivalent discount; PSUs via similar approach or Monte Carlo for market conditions); expense recognition methods for RSUs and PSUs based on service, performance, or market conditions; treatment of retirement eligibility; and periodic adjustments for estimated forfeitures and expected vesting.
- Details income tax accounting using the asset and liability method for deferred taxes on temporary differences and carryforwards at enacted rates; approach to uncertain tax positions (more-likely-than-not threshold and largest benefit recognized), and recording of interest and penalties in income tax expense (not material); notes treatment of state/local taxes as allowable and allocable to government contracts in operating costs, with changes in deferred state taxes and unrecognized state tax benefits recognized in unallocated corporate expenses.
- Defines cash equivalents as highly liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
- Explains receivables as unconditional rights to consideration, recorded at the net amount expected to be collected, with no significant impairments in 2021, 2020, or 2019.
- Defines contract assets as unbilled amounts from percentage-of-completion (cost-to-cost) revenue recognition when revenue exceeds billings; measured at the net amount expected to be billed and collected; classified as current based on the contract operating cycle, even if billing/collection may occur beyond one year due to long-cycle contracts.

nodes.title: Cash and cash equivalents
nodes.heading: Cash and cash equivalents –
nodes.start_phrase: Cash equivalents include highly liquid instruments with original maturities of 90 days or less.
nodes.summary:
- Research and development costs: Distinguishes company-funded (IR&D) from customer-funded R&D; defines included activities (basic/applied research, design, development, testing). Company-funded R&D is allocated to customer contracts as G&A and is generally recoverable on U.S. Government contracts; customer-funded R&D is charged directly to contracts. Substantially all R&D costs are expensed to cost of sales as incurred. Company-funded R&D charged to cost of sales was $1.5 billion in 2021 and $1.3 billion in both 2020 and 2019.

- Stock-based compensation: Awards include RSUs and PSUs that generally vest over three years and settle in shares. Fair value is measured at grant date: RSUs at market price less a dividend-equivalent discount; PSUs similarly or via Monte Carlo when market conditions apply. Expense recognition is straight-line over the requisite service period (which may be shorter than vesting if retirement-eligible) for RSUs; for PSUs, straight-line over vesting with estimates for service/performance outcomes, and straight-line for market-condition PSUs regardless of outcome. Forfeiture estimates and PSU vesting expectations are updated each reporting date.

- Income taxes: Uses the asset and liability method to recognize deferred tax assets/liabilities for temporary differences and carryforwards, measured using enacted rates. Uncertain tax positions are evaluated under a more-likely-than-not threshold, with recognition of the largest benefit more likely than not to be realized; interest and penalties are recorded in income tax expense and were not material. For government contracts, current state/local income and franchise taxes are allowable and recorded in operating costs; changes in deferred state taxes and unrecognized state tax benefits are recognized in unallocated corporate expenses.

nodes.title: Inventories

nodes.title: Property, plant and equipment
nodes.heading: Property, plant and equipment –

- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or estimated net realizable value. Predominantly work-in-process for contracts not yet transferred, comprising labor, materials, subcontractor, and overhead. Useful lives: buildings 10–40 years; machinery/equipment 5–15 years. No depreciation on construction in progress. Depreciation expense: $904M (2021), $853M (2020), $794M (2019). nodes.title: Fair value of financial instruments
nodes.heading: Fair value of financial instruments –
nodes.start_phrase: We measure the fair value of our financial instruments using observable and unobservable inputs.
nodes.summary:
- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or net realizable value; primarily work-in-process for contracts not yet transferred. Pre-contract costs are capitalized as WIP when directly related to a probable, specifically identifiable contract, create/enhance resources for performance, and are recoverable; otherwise expensed. Other inventories use FIFO or average cost. Losses recognized for nonrecoverable pre-contract costs or diminished utility (damage, obsolescence, price changes).

Useful lives: buildings 10–40 years; machinery and equipment 5–15 years. No depreciation for construction-in-progress. Impairment tested upon triggering events using undiscounted cash flows, with write-down to fair value if impaired. Depreciation expense: $904m (2021), $853m (2020), $794m (2019).

nodes.title: Investments
nodes.heading: Investments –
nodes.start_phrase: Substantially all assets measured at fair value represent investments held in a separate trust to fund certain of our non-qualified deferred compensation plan liabilities.
nodes.summary:
- Inventories: Carried at lower of cost or estimated net realizable value. Majority is work-in-process (labor, material, subcontractor, overhead) for contracts where control hasn’t transferred. Pre-contract costs are capitalized as WIP only if tied to an identifiable probable award, directly related to the contract, create/enhance resources for performance, and are recoverable; expensed upon transfer of products/services after award. Other pre-contract and start-up costs are expensed as incurred. Other inventory (materials, spares, supplies) uses FIFO or average cost. Losses recognized for nonrecoverable pre-contract costs or diminished utility (damage, obsolescence, price changes).
- Contract liabilities: Advance payments and billings in excess of recognized revenue; classified as current based on contract operating cycle and presented net of revenue recognized on a contract-by-contract basis at period end.
- Property, plant and equipment: Recorded at cost; accelerated depreciation in first half of useful life then straight-line thereafter. Useful lives: buildings 10–40 years; machinery/equipment 5–15 years. No depreciation on construction in progress. Depreciation expense: $904m (2021), $853m (2020), $794m (2019). - Capitalized software: Internal-use software costs capitalized in other noncurrent assets; amortized straight-line over 2–6 years once ready for intended use. Net balances: $777m (2021) and $686m (2020); accumulated amortization $2.3b (2021) and $2.2b (2020). Amortization expense: $175m (2021), $166m (2020), $111m (2019).

- Investments (deferred compensation trust): Substantially all fair value assets fund non-qualified deferred compensation liabilities; fair value $2.1b (2021) and $2.0b (2020) in other noncurrent assets. Most measured at cost adjusted for observable price changes or impairment; Level 1 at fair value each period. Carrying amounts: $465m (2021) and $173m (2020) in other assets (current and noncurrent). 2021 net gains $265m ($199m after-tax, $0.72/share) in other non-operating income, net; no net gains in 2020.

Share of investee results recorded in operating profit within other income, net. Impairment recognized for other-than-temporary declines. Balances: $689m (2021) and $784m (2020), primarily United Launch Alliance. Share of net earnings: $97m (2021), $163m (2020), $154m (2019); Space segment included approx. $67m, $135m, and $145m, respectively. AMMROC stake sale: agreement in July 2020 for $307m; recognized $128m noncash impairment ($96m after-tax, $0.34/share) in 2020; sale completed Nov 25, 2020 with full cash proceeds.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: Acquisitions recorded at fair value. Goodwill is excess over identifiable net assets; intangible assets include customer programs, trademarks, customer relationships, technology, etc., amortized over 5–20 years. Goodwill balance $10.8b at Dec 31, 2021 and 2020. Goodwill tested at the reporting unit level at least annually (Q4) or upon triggering events, using qualitative screening or quantitative testing. Quantitative tests rely on DCF and market-based methods (comparable companies and transactions), requiring judgments on future cash flows, growth, discount rates, and valuation multiples, considering market conditions, U.S. Government budgets, orders, supplier contracts, and labor agreements.

nodes.title: Equity method investments
nodes.heading: Equity method investments –
nodes.start_phrase: Investments where we have the ability to exercise significant influence, but do not control, are accounted for under the equity method of accounting and are included in other noncurrent assets on our consolidated balance sheets.
nodes.summary:
- Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund investments: carried within other assets (current and noncurrent); fair values of $465 million (2021) and $173 million (2020). Recorded $265 million of net gains in 2021 ($199 million after-tax, $0.72 per share) from fair value changes/sales, reflected in other non-operating income, net; no net gains in 2020.
- Equity method investments: applied when significant influence exists (typically 20%–50% ownership); recorded in other noncurrent assets. Share of investees’ earnings/losses recognized in operating profit within other income, net, aligned with the related business segment. Impairment assessed when indicators arise; other-than-temporary declines recognized in earnings. Balances of $689 million (2021) and $784 million (2020), primarily United Launch Alliance (ULA). Share of net earnings: $97 million (2021), $163 million (2020), $154 million (2019); approximately $67 million, $135 million, and $145 million, respectively, included in Space segment operating profit.
- AMMROC divestiture: agreement in July 2020 to sell ownership interest for $307 million; carrying value adjusted to sale price, resulting in a $128 million noncash impairment ($96 million after-tax, $0.34 per share) in 2020; sale closed November 25, 2020 with cash proceeds received.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: acquisition accounting at fair value; goodwill is excess over identifiable net assets. Intangibles include customer programs, trademarks, customer relationships, technology, and others; amortized over 5–20 years.
- Goodwill balance: $10.8 billion at December 31, 2021 and 2020. Impairment testing performed at least annually (Q4) or upon triggering events (e.g., economic/industry changes, market cap decline, performance, competition, reorganizations, U.S. Government budget constraints, disposals). Goodwill tested at the reporting unit level (business segment or below) where discrete financials exist and results are regularly reviewed.
- Impairment methodology: qualitative assessment to determine likelihood of impairment; if not more likely than not that fair value exceeds carrying amount, a quantitative test is performed. Quantitative tests conducted for most reporting units at least every three years, some annually. Fair value estimated using DCF and market approaches (comparable company multiples and transaction multiples); key judgments include projected cash flows, long-term growth, discount rates, and relevant market multiples. Cash flows reflect best estimates based on market conditions, U.S. Government budgets, firm and expected orders, supplier contracts, and labor agreements.

nodes.title: Goodwill and Intangible Assets
nodes.heading: Goodwill and Intangible Assets –
nodes.start_phrase: The assets and liabilities of acquired businesses are recorded under the acquisition method of accounting at their estimated fair values at the date of acquisition.
nodes.summary:
- Fair value investments: Lockheed Martin Ventures Fund holdings were $465 million (2021) and $173 million (2020), recorded in other assets. In 2021, the company recognized $265 million of net gains ($199 million after-tax; $0.72 per share) from fair value changes/sales, reported in other non-operating income, net; no gains in 2020.
- Equity method investments: Used for holdings with significant influence (generally 20%–50% ownership), recorded in other noncurrent assets; share of investee results recognized in operating profit within other income, net. Balances totaled $689 million (2021) and $784 million (2020), primarily United Launch Alliance (ULA). Share of net earnings was $97 million (2021), $163 million (2020), and $154 million (2019), with approximately $67 million, $135 million, and $145 million, respectively, in the Space segment. The company recorded a $128 million noncash impairment ($96 million after-tax; $0.34 per share) in 2020 tied to the sale of its AMMROC interest for $307 million, completed November 25, 2020.
- Goodwill and intangible assets: Business combinations recorded at fair value; goodwill reflects excess purchase price; identifiable intangibles include customer programs, relationships, trademarks, and technology, amortized over 5–20 years. Goodwill was $10.8 billion at December 31, 2021 and 2020. The company performs annual (Q4) or trigger-based goodwill impairment tests using qualitative or quantitative methods; quantitative tests use DCF and market approaches with judgments about cash flows, growth, discount rates (WACC), and market multiples. No goodwill impairments were identified in 2019–2021. Indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually (not amortized); finite-lived intangibles are amortized 5–20 years and tested upon indicators of impairment.
- Leases: Predominantly long-term operating leases; right-of-use (ROU) assets recorded in other noncurrent assets; lease liabilities in other current/noncurrent liabilities. Both measured at the present value of lease payments using the company’s incremental borrowing rate when no implicit rate exists. Options to extend/terminate included when reasonably certain; expense recognized straight-line in cost of sales. Lease and non-lease components are combined; a portfolio approach is applied for certain equipment; ROU assets are tested for impairment consistent with PPE policy.
- Postretirement benefit plans: Defined benefit pensions, retiree medical/life, and other postemployment benefits measured via actuarial valuations using key assumptions (discount rate, expected long-term asset returns, mortality, health care cost trends, turnover). Asset gains/losses are smoothed over three years to determine market-related value; corridor method amortizes amounts exceeding 10% of the greater of plan assets or obligations. Funded status (fair value of assets minus benefit obligation) is recognized on the balance sheet as a noncurrent asset or liability under GAAP; ERISA funded status is determined on a different basis.

nodes.title: Leases
nodes.heading: Leases –
nodes.start_phrase: We evaluate whether our contractual arrangements contain leases at the inception of such arrangements.
nodes.summary:
- Describes the goodwill impairment testing methodology, including use of discounted cash flow analysis with reporting unit–specific WACC reflecting capital structure and risk; defines reporting unit carrying value components; notes that annual tests in 2019–2021 resulted in no impairments.
- Explains accounting for intangible assets: indefinite-lived intangibles are not amortized but tested annually for impairment and reduced to fair value if needed; finite-lived intangibles are amortized over 5–20 years based on economic benefit patterns and tested for impairment upon triggering events.
- Details lease accounting policies: assessment of whether arrangements contain leases based on control and right to economic benefits; predominance of long-term operating leases and lack of significant finance leases; recognition of right-of-use operating lease assets and corresponding liabilities at lease commencement at the present value of lease payments.
- Specifies measurement inputs for leases: use of incremental borrowing rate when no implicit rate is available; inclusion of payments made at or before commencement net of incentives; classification of ROU assets in other noncurrent assets and liabilities split between other current and other noncurrent liabilities.
- Addresses lease term options: inclusion of extension or termination options when reasonably certain; recognition of operating lease expense on a straight-line basis in cost of sales.
- Notes treatment of lease and non-lease components: accounted for as a single component due to insignificance of non-lease elements; portfolio approach applied for certain equipment leases; ROU assets evaluated for impairment consistent with property, plant, and equipment policy.
- Outlines postretirement benefit plan accounting for defined benefit pensions, retiree medical and life insurance, and other postemployment benefits using actuarial valuations based on key assumptions (discount rate, expected long-term return on assets, mortality/longevity, healthcare cost trends, employee turnover).
- Describes smoothing mechanisms: market-related value of plan assets based on actual gains/losses over three years; amortization of deferred gains/losses using the corridor method when they exceed 10% of the greater of plan assets or benefit obligations.
- Explains recognition of funded status on a plan-by-plan basis as an asset or liability on the balance sheet, measured as the difference between fair value of assets and benefit obligation under GAAP, and notes that ERISA funded status is calculated differently.

nodes.title: Postretirement benefit plans
nodes.heading: Postretirement benefit plans –
nodes.start_phrase: Many of our employees and retirees participate in defined benefit pension plans, retiree medical and life insurance plans, and other postemployment plans (collectively, postretirement benefit plans).
nodes.summary:
- Goodwill and intangible assets: Describes annual impairment testing using discounted cash flow analyses based on each reporting unit’s WACC; reporting unit carrying values include operating assets/liabilities, goodwill, and certain allocations. Notes that 2019–2021 goodwill tests showed no impairment. Indefinite-lived intangibles are tested annually (no amortization); finite-lived intangibles are amortized over 5–20 years and tested for impairment upon triggering events.

- Lease accounting: Explains identification of leases and predominance of long-term operating leases. Details recognition of right-of-use (ROU) assets (other noncurrent assets) and operating lease liabilities (current/noncurrent) measured at the present value of lease payments using the incremental borrowing rate. Addresses options to extend/terminate when reasonably certain, straight-line lease expense in cost of sales, combining lease and non-lease components, portfolio approach for certain equipment, and impairment evaluation of ROU assets.

- Postretirement benefit plans: Outlines actuarial valuation approach, key assumptions (discount rate, expected long-term return on assets, mortality, health care cost trends, turnover), use of a market-related value of assets with three-year smoothing, and corridor amortization when gains/losses exceed 10% of the greater of plan assets or obligations. States GAAP recognition of funded status on the balance sheet and notes differences between GAAP and ERISA measures.

- Postemployment plans: Provides recognition criteria for severance and similar benefits. Discloses specific charges: 2021 restructuring in the RMS segment ($36 million; $28 million after-tax, $0.10 per share) for workforce reductions and facility exits; 2020 corporate severance ($27 million; $21 million after-tax, $0.08 per share), with lump-sum payments based on service.
